newsitem.title: JAPAN: Scandal probe closes in on Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank.
newsitem.headline: Scandal probe closes in on Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank.

text.p: Japanese authorities moved against scandal-tainted Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank on Friday, indicting its former chairman and lodging criminal complaints against the bank and four former officials.

The Ministry of Finance (MOF) filed complaints with Tokyo prosecutors alleging DKB and the officials violated the country's Banking Law, a move that paves the way for administrative and possibly criminal penalties against what is Japan's third-biggest bank in terms of assets.

Financial sources said the alleged violations included concealing information about bank loans to a corporate racketeer at the centre of a financial scandal which has also embroiled Nomura Securities Co Ltd, Japan's biggest brokerage.
Prosecutors indicted former DKB chairman Tadashi Okuda on suspicion of making illegal loans to the "sokaiya" racketeer, Ryuichi Koike.

The indictment accuses Okuda, 65, of extending 11.78 billion yen ($101 million) in loans to Koike from DKB through Tokyo-based financial firm Daiwa Shinyo in about 52 installments between July 7, 1994, and September 6, 1996.
Okuda is the latest in a series of former executives from DKB and Nomura to be indicted in the scandal, which is unfolding just as Japan begins "Big Bang" reforms of its financial sector.
Now MOF has filed a complaint, prosecutors are likely to indict DKB itself, possibly next week, for breaking the Banking Law, Japanese media reports said.
The ministry is expected to announce administrative penalties against Nomura, and possibly DKB, next week.

The penalty for Nomura for violating the Securities and Exchange Law with illegal stock trades could include a suspension of all or part of its operations for up to six months or a revoking of its securities licences.

Financial analysts said the Nomura penalties are likely be the heaviest-ever imposed on a securities firm as it also violated the Commercial Code by making payoffs to a racketeer using funds raised through shady stock deals.
Some speculate Nomura could face a partial suspension of its operations for four to five months.
MOF's punishment of DKB would be decided based on what prosecutors discover in their investigations into the bank, a financial source said.
The Finance Ministry's complaint alleges that the bank itself committed violations of the Banking Law, not only the four former officials, the source said.
DKB is alleged to have concealed information on loans it made to racketeer Koike when the ministry carried out an inspection of the bank in October 1994, he added.

It is the first time the ministry has filed a complaint seeking criminal charges against a bank. However, under current criminal law, the maximum penalty for such a violation is paltry 500,000 yen ($4,310) fine.

Payoffs to sokaiya -- corporate racketeers who buy shares in companies and try to extort money by threatening to expose dubious business practices, or who are sometimes employed by firms to quash questions from legitimate shareholders at annual meetings -- have been illegal since 1983.
But many Japanese companies have found it difficult to cut the ties that bind them to the underworld. ($1=116 yen)
